questions.text:
Differentiate f(x) = √(4 – 9x⁴).

You do not need to simplify your answer.
questions.markingGuide: Apply chain rule: f′(x) = ½(4 – 9x⁴)^(–½) × (–36x³) = –18x³(4 – 9x⁴)^(–½). Or equivalent form. Achieved = correct derivative.

questions.text:
A curve is defined by the equation y = (x² + 3x + 2) sin x.

Find the gradient of the tangent to this curve when x = 0.

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: Product rule: dy/dx = (2x + 3) sin x + (x² + 3x + 2) cos x. Substitute x = 0: dy/dx = 3 × 0 + 2 × 1 = 2. Achieved = correct gradient of tangent with correct derivative. Merit = finds the correct inequality for required values of x for a decreasing function, with evidence of derivative.

questions.text:
For the function below, find the range of values of x for which the function is decreasing.

y = 3(2x – 7)² + 60 ln x + 12, x > 0

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: dy/dx = 6(2x – 7) × 2 + 60/x = 12(2x – 7) + 60/x. Decreasing when dy/dx < 0. Multiply through by x (positive): 12x(2x – 7) + 60 < 0 gives 24x² – 84x + 60 < 0, so 2x² – 7x + 5 < 0, factorises as (2x – 5)(x – 1) < 0, giving 1 < x < 2.5. Achieved = evidence of reaching stage (1), can set = 0 and find the correct critical values for (a). Merit = finds the correct inequality for required values of x for a decreasing function, with evidence of derivative.

questions.text:
Find the x-value(s) of any stationary points on the graph of the function below, and determine their nature.

y = (2x – 1)e^(–2x)

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: dy/dx = 2e^(–2x) + (2x – 1)(–2)e^(–2x) = e^(–2x)(2 – 4x + 2) = e^(–2x)(4 – 4x). Set dy/dx = 0: e^(–2x)(4 – 4x) = 0. Since e^(–2x) ≠ 0, 4 – 4x = 0 so x = 1. d²y/dx² = e^(–2x)(8x – 12). At x = 1: d²y/dx² = e^(–2)(–4) ≈ –0.541 < 0, so maximum. Achieved = correct expression for dy/dx. Merit = finds x = 1 and justifies this is a maximum using a calculus method, and with evidence of derivative.

questions.text:
A curve is defined by the equation y = (2x² – 1 – 2x ln x) / x, where x > 0.

The curve has a point of inflection at the point P.

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point P.

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: Simplify: y = 2x – x⁻¹ – 2 ln x. dy/dx = 2 + x⁻² – 2/x. d²y/dx² = –2x⁻³ + 2x⁻². For inflection, d²y/dx² = 0: –2/x³ + 2/x² = 0, so 2x³ = 2x², giving x = 1 (ignoring x = 0). At x = 1: y = 1, dy/dx = 1. Tangent: y – 1 = 1(x – 1), so y = x. Achieved = correct expression for dy/dx. Merit = finds x = 1 with correct d²y/dx² and dy/dx. E7/T1 = consistent equation of tangent from incorrect P, or correct solution but with one minor error. E8/T2 = correct equation of tangent found.

questions.text:
A function is defined parametrically by the pair of equations:

x = 3t² + 1 and y = cos t.

Find an expression for dy/dx.
questions.markingGuide: dx/dt = 6t, dy/dt = –sin t. dy/dx = (dy/dt) / (dx/dt) = –sin t / (6t). Achieved = correct expression for dy/dx. dy/dx can be expressed in terms of x, y.

questions.text:
An object is travelling in a straight line. Its displacement, in metres, is given by the formula

s(t) = ln(3t² + 5t + 2), where t > 0 and t is time, in seconds.

Find the velocity of this object when t = 1 second.

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: ds/dt = v = (6t + 5) / (3t² + 5t + 2). At t = 1: v = 11/10 = 1.1 m s⁻¹. Achieved = correct derivative AND correct value for velocity of v = 11/10 = 1.1. Units not required.

questions.text:
Show that y = sin(x²) – cos(x) is a solution to the equation

d²y/dx² + 4x²y = 2cos(x²) + (1 – 4x²)cos x.
questions.markingGuide: dy/dx = 2x cos(x²) + sin x. d²y/dx² = 2cos(x²) – 4x² sin(x²) + cos x. Then d²y/dx² + 4x²y = 2cos(x²) – 4x² sin(x²) + cos x + 4x²(sin(x²) – cos x) = 2cos(x²) + cos x – 4x² cos x = 2cos(x²) + (1 – 4x²)cos x = RHS. Achieved = correct expression for dy/dx. Excellence = correct justification that it is a solution, with evidence of both dy/dx and d²y/dx².

questions.text:
Consider the function f(x) = (ln x) / x, x > 0.

Find the coordinates of the point of inflection on the graph of the function.

You can assume that your point found is actually a point of inflection.

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: f′(x) = (1 – ln x) / x². f″(x) = (–3 + 2 ln x) / x³. For inflection: f″(x) = 0 gives –3 + 2 ln x = 0, so ln x = 3/2, x = e^(3/2) ≈ 4.4817. y = 1.5 × e^(–1.5) ≈ 0.3347. Achieved = correct expression for f′(x). Merit = correct expression for f″(x). Excellence = correct coordinates of point of inflection, with evidence of both dy/dx and d²y/dx².

questions.text:
The graph of the function y = xe^(3x) / (2x + k), where k is a non-zero constant, has a single turning point at Q.

Find the x-coordinate of the point Q.

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: dy/dx = [e^(3x)(6x² + 3kx + k)] / (2x + k)². Setting dy/dx = 0: e^(3x)(6x² + 3kx + k) = 0. Since e^(3x) ≠ 0, solve 6x² + 3kx + k = 0. For a single turning point, discriminant = 0: (3k)² – 4(6)(k) = 0, so 9k² – 24k = 0, giving 3k(3k – 8) = 0. Since k ≠ 0, k = 8/3. Substituting: 6x² + 8x + 8/3 = 0, so 18x² + 24x + 8 = 0, giving 9x² + 12x + 4 = 0, (3x + 2)² = 0, x = –⅔. Achieved = correct dy/dx. Merit = finds the correct value of k, with evidence of calculus methods. E7/T1 = correct solution but with one minor error. E8/T2 = calculates x-coordinate of Q, with clear and full calculus justification.

questions.text:
Differentiate y = √x · sec(6x).

You do not need to simplify your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: dy/dx = ½ x^(–½) sec(6x) + 6x^(½) sec(6x) tan(6x)
questions.markingGuide: Product rule with chain rule on sec(6x): dy/dx = ½ x^(–½) sec(6x) + √x · 6 sec(6x) tan(6x). Or equivalent. Achieved = correct derivative.

questions.text:
Find the x-value(s) of any stationary point(s) on the graph of the function f(x) = (x² – 5x + 4) / (x² + 5x + 4).

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
You do not need to determine the nature of any stationary point(s) found.
questions.markingGuide: f′(x) = [(2x – 5)(x² + 5x + 4) – (x² – 5x + 4)(2x + 5)] / (x² + 5x + 4)². Numerator simplifies to 10x² – 40 = 10(x² – 4). Set f′(x) = 0: x² – 4 = 0, so x = 2 or x = –2. Achieved = correct expression for f′(x). Merit = x-values of both stationary points found, with evidence of a calculus method.

questions.text:
Jamie is doing some baking and pouring the flour to form a conical pile.

The height of the pile is always the same as the diameter of the base of the cone.

If the flour is being added at a constant rate of 3 cm³ per second, at what rate is the height increasing when the pile is 4 cm in height?

You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.

Note that volume of a cone = ⅓πr²h.
questions.markingGuide: Since h = 2r, r = h/2. V = ⅓π(h/2)²h = πh³/12. dV/dh = πh²/4. Using dh/dt = (dh/dV)(dV/dt) = (4/(πh²)) × 3. At h = 4: dh/dt = 12/(16π) = 3/(4π) ≈ 0.2387 cm s⁻¹. Achieved = correct expression for dV/dr or dV/dh. Merit = correct value for dh/dt with evidence of a calculus method.

questions.text:
The diagram below shows part of the graph of the function f(x) = e^(–x²), where x ≥ 0.

The point P lies on the curve and the point Q lies on the x-axis so that OP = PQ, where O is the origin.

Prove that the largest possible area of the triangle OPQ is 1/√(2e).

You do not need to show that the area you have found is a maximum.
You must use calculus and show any derivatives that you need to find when solving this problem.
questions.markingGuide: Let P have coordinates (x, y) where y = e^(–x²). Area of triangle OPQ = ½x × e^(–x²) (since base = 2x on x-axis). dA/dx = ½ e^(–x²)(1 – 2x²). Set dA/dx = 0: e^(–x²)(1 – 2x²) = 0. Since e^(–x²) ≠ 0, 1 – 2x² = 0 so x = 1/√2. Ignore x = –1/√2 as x > 0. Area = ½ × (1/√2) × e^(–½) = 1/(2√2) × 1/√e = 1/√(2e). E7/T1 = correct proof but with one minor error. E8/T2 = correct proof of exact area value with evidence of a calculus method.
